examples.knowledge_point: Multiplying a Matrix by a Column or Row of the Identity Matrix
examples.problem:
Calculate the product $C D,$ if
$[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -4 \\ 5 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}]$
and 
$[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
examples.worked_solution:
Notice that $D$ is the $2$nd *column* of the identity matrix $I_3.$

Since we're multiplying the $3\times 3$ matrix $C$ by the $2$nd *column* of the identity matrix $I_3,$ the result must be the $2$nd *column* of $C.$ Therefore,

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Don't believe it? Let's check the long way:

$$
\begin{aligned}CD & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -4 \\ 5 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 0+1\cdot 1+0\cdot 0 \\ -1\cdot 0+1\cdot 1+(-4)\cdot 0 \\ 5\cdot 0+4\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Calculate the product ${I}_{2}G$ given that ${I}_{2}$ is the $2\times 2$ identity matrix and
$G=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -5\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
Any matrix, when multiplied by an identity matrix, remains unchanged (assuming that the multiplication is well defined).

The matrix ${I}_{2}$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $G$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix too. 

Therefore, the multiplication is well defined and 

$$
{I}_{2}\cdot G=G=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$
